newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Controversial Ukrainian ex-PM returns from Israel.
newsitem.headline: Controversial Ukrainian ex-PM returns from Israel.

text.p: Former Ukrainian prime minister Yefim Zvyagilsky, once accused of embezzling $25 million of public money, has returned to his home town after more than two years in Israel, local officials in Donetsk said on Tuesday.
"Yefim Leonidovich (Zvyagilsky) returned to Donetsk yesterday and he was here today," said an official at Ukraine's largest coalmine, where the ex-premier was once director.

He told Reuters by telephone that Zvyagilsky, who had his parliamentary immunity from prosecution restored last month, had toured the Zasyadko pit at Donetsk, the heart of Ukraine's coal industry, 500 km (300 miles) from the capital Kiev.
Zvyagilsky also used to be mayor of Donetsk and still holds a parliamentary seat for the city.
"He was greeted by thousands of miners at two separate rallies and is going to go down into the mine. People are happy and he was welcomed with lots of cheering," the official said.

Ukrainian deputies voted last month to restore the former premier's parliamentary immunity, clearing the way for his return from Israel, where he had spent the last two and a half years. Parliament then stipulated Zvyagilsky must return to Kiev within two months or lose his immunity from prosecution.
Zvyagilsky, 64, was acting prime minister for nine months from 1993 to 1994 under Ukraine's first post-Soviet president, Leonid Kravchuk.
He stands accused of siphoning off state funds through the illegal sale of 200,000 tonnes of aviation fuel and foreign exchange operations involving a bank set up by his wife.
Zvyagilsky rejected the allegations and accused the former prosecutor-general of "political retaliation."
"We will work together. I am very glad to be here. Thank you for waiting for me. You didn't abandon me during my absence," the official quoted Zvyagilsky as telling miners at the rally.

The former government leader also said he would continue to sit in parliament but would never again take an official post in Kiev, calling his decision to serve as prime minister "the biggest mistake of my life".
Zvyagilsky has said he has not taken Israeli citizenship. Many thousands of his fellow Jewish Ukrainians have emigrated to Israel since the collapse of the Soviet Union.
